claim: Distal apical trunk dendrites of CA3 pyramidal cells exhibit distinct forms of dendritic Ca2+ spikes, unlike CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Using dendritic patch-clamp recordings and two-photon Ca2+ imaging in acute slices from male rats, we report that, unlike CA1PCs, distal apical trunk dendrites of CA3PCs exhibit distinct forms of dendritic Ca2+ spikes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dendritic patch-clamp recordings and two-photon Ca2+ imaging comparing CA3PCs and CA1PCs.

claim: CA3 pyramidal cells express ADP-type global Ca2+ spikes.
source: Besides ADP-type global Ca2+ spikes, a majority of dendrites expresses a novel, fast Ca2+ spike type that is initiated locally without bAPs, can recruit additional Na+ currents, and is compartmentalized to the activated dendritic subtree.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from dendritic recordings.

claim: A majority of CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites express a novel, fast Ca2+ spike type that is initiated locally without backpropagating action potentials.
source: Besides ADP-type global Ca2+ spikes, a majority of dendrites expresses a novel, fast Ca2+ spike type that is initiated locally without bAPs, can recruit additional Na+ currents, and is compartmentalized to the activated dendritic subtree.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dendritic recordings showing fast Ca2+ spikes without bAPs.

claim: The novel fast Ca2+ spike type in CA3 pyramidal cells can recruit additional Na+ currents.
source: Besides ADP-type global Ca2+ spikes, a majority of dendrites expresses a novel, fast Ca2+ spike type that is initiated locally without bAPs, can recruit additional Na+ currents, and is compartmentalized to the activated dendritic subtree.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the involvement of Na+ currents in the fast Ca2+ spike.

claim: The novel fast Ca2+ spike type is compartmentalized to the activated dendritic subtree.
source: Besides ADP-type global Ca2+ spikes, a majority of dendrites expresses a novel, fast Ca2+ spike type that is initiated locally without bAPs, can recruit additional Na+ currents, and is compartmentalized to the activated dendritic subtree.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing spatial restriction of the fast Ca2+ spike.

claim: Occurrence of different Ca2+ spike types correlates with dendritic structure in CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: Occurrence of the different Ca2+ spike types correlates with dendritic structure, indicating morpho-functional heterogeneity among CA3PCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between spike types and morphological features.

claim: Different Ca2+ spike types indicate morpho-functional heterogeneity among CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: Occurrence of the different Ca2+ spike types correlates with dendritic structure, indicating morpho-functional heterogeneity among CA3PCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between spike types and dendritic structure.

claim: ADP-type Ca2+ spikes produce burst firing at the soma.
source: Importantly, ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes produce opposing somatic output: bursts versus strictly single-action potentials, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dual soma-dendrite recordings.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes produce strictly single action potentials at the soma.
source: Importantly, ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes produce opposing somatic output: bursts versus strictly single-action potentials, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dual soma-dendrite recordings.

claim: The variability of dendritic Ca2+ spikes may underlie heterogeneous input-output transformation and bursting properties of CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: The uncovered variability of dendritic Ca2+ spikes may underlie heterogeneous input-output transformation and bursting properties of CA3PCs, and might specifically contribute to key associative and non-associative computations performed by the CA3 network.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed variability of Ca2+ spikes and their effects on output.

claim: The variability of dendritic Ca2+ spikes might contribute to associative and non-associative computations performed by the CA3 network.
source: The uncovered variability of dendritic Ca2+ spikes may underlie heterogeneous input-output transformation and bursting properties of CA3PCs, and might specifically contribute to key associative and non-associative computations performed by the CA3 network.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role for the observed Ca2+ spike variability.

claim: Cortical pyramidal cell dendrites support multiple types of regenerative dendritic spikes including Na+ spikes, NMDA spikes, and Ca2+ spikes.
source: In particular, cortical pyramidal cell (PC) dendrites are thought to support multiple types of regenerative dendritic spikes (d-spikes), including Na+ spikes (mediated by voltage-gated Na+ channels [VGNCs]), NMDA spikes (mediated by NMDARs), and Ca2+ spikes (mediated by voltage-gated Ca2+ channels [VGCCs]) (Stuart and Spruston, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stuart and Spruston, 2015.

claim: Na+ and NMDA spikes can be generated locally in individual thin dendrites of pyramidal cells.
source: While Na+ and NMDA spikes can be generated locally in individual thin dendrites of PCs (Ariav et al., 2003; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Makara and Magee, 2013; Nevian et al., 2007; Polsky et al., 2004), Ca2+ spikes are thought to represent mostly global dendritic events that are responsible for bursting (Francioni and Harnett, 2021; London and Häusser, 2005; Magee and Carruth, 1999; Stuart and Spruston, 2015; Stuyt et al., 2021; Williams and Stuart, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Ariav et al., 2003; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Makara and Magee, 2013; Nevian et al., 2007; Polsky et al., 2004).

claim: Ca2+ spikes are thought to represent mostly global dendritic events that are responsible for bursting.
source: While Na+ and NMDA spikes can be generated locally in individual thin dendrites of PCs (Ariav et al., 2003; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Makara and Magee, 2013; Nevian et al., 2007; Polsky et al., 2004), Ca2+ spikes are thought to represent mostly global dendritic events that are responsible for bursting (Francioni and Harnett, 2021; London and Häusser, 2005; Magee and Carruth, 1999; Stuart and Spruston, 2015; Stuyt et al., 2021; Williams and Stuart, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Francioni and Harnett, 2021; London and Häusser, 2005; Magee and Carruth, 1999; Stuart and Spruston, 2015; Stuyt et al., 2021; Williams and Stuart, 1999).

claim: In CA1 pyramidal cells and neocortical layer 5 pyramidal cells, Ca2+ spikes are generated in the main apical trunk upon widespread synaptic depolarization in distal dendrites concomitant with backpropagating action potentials.
source: Studies in hippocampal CA1PCs and neocortical layer 5 PCs (L5PCs) have shown that Ca2+ spikes are generated in the main apical trunk efficiently upon widespread synaptic depolarization in distal (tuft) dendrites concomitant with backpropagating action potentials (bAPs), and manifest as an afterdepolarization (ADP) producing a characteristic burst of additional APs (also called complex spike burst [CSB]) at the soma (Harnett et al., 2013; Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum et al., 1999; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Harnett et al., 2013; Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum et al., 1999; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).

claim: Ca2+ spikes in CA1 and L5 pyramidal cells manifest as an afterdepolarization producing a characteristic burst of additional action potentials at the soma.
source: Studies in hippocampal CA1PCs and neocortical layer 5 PCs (L5PCs) have shown that Ca2+ spikes are generated in the main apical trunk efficiently upon widespread synaptic depolarization in distal (tuft) dendrites concomitant with backpropagating action potentials (bAPs), and manifest as an afterdepolarization (ADP) producing a characteristic burst of additional APs (also called complex spike burst [CSB]) at the soma (Harnett et al., 2013; Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum et al., 1999; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Harnett et al., 2013; Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum et al., 1999; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).

claim: Ca2+ spikes can act as an associative dendritic signal that translates coincident activation of proximal and distal input pathways into a burst output.
source: These results led to a concept that Ca2+ spikes can act as an associative dendritic signal that translates a specific input pattern (coincident activation of proximal and distal input pathways) into a burst output (a reliable form of downstream synaptic information transfer; Lisman, 1997) and induce synaptic plasticity (Bittner et al., 2017; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Lisman, 1997; Bittner et al., 2017; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).

claim: Ca2+ spikes can induce synaptic plasticity.
source: These results led to a concept that Ca2+ spikes can act as an associative dendritic signal that translates a specific input pattern (coincident activation of proximal and distal input pathways) into a burst output (a reliable form of downstream synaptic information transfer; Lisman, 1997) and induce synaptic plasticity (Bittner et al., 2017; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Bittner et al., 2017; Takahashi and Magee, 2009).

claim: CA3 pyramidal cells play a fundamental role in hippocampal associative learning and memory functions.
source: These neurons play a fundamental role in hippocampal associative learning and memory functions (Kesner, 2013; Marr, 1971; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Nakazawa et al., 2002; Rolls, 2007), forming a recurrent network governed by input from the dentate gyrus via mossy fibers (MFs) and the entorhinal cortex (EC) (Witter, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Kesner, 2013; Marr, 1971; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Nakazawa et al., 2002; Rolls, 2007).

claim: CA3 pyramidal cells form a recurrent network governed by input from the dentate gyrus via mossy fibers and the entorhinal cortex.
source: These neurons play a fundamental role in hippocampal associative learning and memory functions (Kesner, 2013; Marr, 1971; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Nakazawa et al., 2002; Rolls, 2007), forming a recurrent network governed by input from the dentate gyrus via mossy fibers (MFs) and the entorhinal cortex (EC) (Witter, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Witter, 2007).

claim: CA3 pyramidal cells frequently produce bursts of action potentials both in vivo and in vitro.
source: CA3PCs frequently produce bursts of APs both in vivo and in vitro (Ding et al., 2020; Hablitz and Johnston, 1981; Hunt et al., 2018; Kowalski et al., 2016; Mizuseki et al., 2012; Oliva et al., 2016; Raus Balind et al., 2019; Wong and Prince, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Ding et al., 2020; Hablitz and Johnston, 1981; Hunt et al., 2018; Kowalski et al., 2016; Mizuseki et al., 2012; Oliva et al., 2016; Raus Balind et al., 2019; Wong and Prince, 1978).

claim: CA3 pyramidal cells are heterogeneous regarding their intrinsic complex spike burst firing propensity.
source: Investigating CSB generation in CA3PCs, we have recently reported (Raus Balind et al., 2019) that CA3PCs are heterogeneous regarding their intrinsic CSB firing propensity, and the required synaptic input patterns for evoking CSBs can be diverse as well: while in a subset of CA3PCs associative inputs drive bursts, in other CA3PCs even inputs restricted to single dendrites can efficiently produce CSBs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Raus Balind et al., 2019).

claim: The required synaptic input patterns for evoking complex spike bursts in CA3 pyramidal cells can be diverse.
source: Investigating CSB generation in CA3PCs, we have recently reported (Raus Balind et al., 2019) that CA3PCs are heterogeneous regarding their intrinsic CSB firing propensity, and the required synaptic input patterns for evoking CSBs can be diverse as well: while in a subset of CA3PCs associative inputs drive bursts, in other CA3PCs even inputs restricted to single dendrites can efficiently produce CSBs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Raus Balind et al., 2019).

claim: In a subset of CA3 pyramidal cells, associative inputs drive bursts.
source: Investigating CSB generation in CA3PCs, we have recently reported (Raus Balind et al., 2019) that CA3PCs are heterogeneous regarding their intrinsic CSB firing propensity, and the required synaptic input patterns for evoking CSBs can be diverse as well: while in a subset of CA3PCs associative inputs drive bursts, in other CA3PCs even inputs restricted to single dendrites can efficiently produce CSBs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Raus Balind et al., 2019).

claim: In some CA3 pyramidal cells, inputs restricted to single dendrites can efficiently produce complex spike bursts.
source: Investigating CSB generation in CA3PCs, we have recently reported (Raus Balind et al., 2019) that CA3PCs are heterogeneous regarding their intrinsic CSB firing propensity, and the required synaptic input patterns for evoking CSBs can be diverse as well: while in a subset of CA3PCs associative inputs drive bursts, in other CA3PCs even inputs restricted to single dendrites can efficiently produce CSBs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Raus Balind et al., 2019).

claim: Early studies using blind microelectrode recordings observed putative dendritic Ca2+ spikes to which bursting was attributed in CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: Early studies using blind microelectrode recordings observed putative dendritic Ca2+ spikes to which bursting was attributed (Nuñez and Buño, 1992; Wong et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Nuñez and Buño, 1992; Wong et al., 1979).

claim: Direct patch-clamp recordings in CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites revealed and dissected Na+ and NMDA spikes.
source: Later, direct patch-clamp recordings in CA3PC dendrites revealed and dissected Na+ and NMDA spikes (Brandalise et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2012; Makara and Magee, 2013), but Ca2+ spikes have not been specifically examined.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Brandalise et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2012; Makara and Magee, 2013).

claim: Ca2+ spikes in CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites have not been specifically examined prior to this study.
source: Later, direct patch-clamp recordings in CA3PC dendrites revealed and dissected Na+ and NMDA spikes (Brandalise et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2012; Makara and Magee, 2013), but Ca2+ spikes have not been specifically examined.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of prior studies specifically examining Ca2+ spikes in CA3PC dendrites.

claim: The primary apical trunk of CA3 pyramidal cells bifurcates after a relatively short distance into multiple higher-order intermediate branches.
source: Intriguingly, unlike several widely studied PC types (e.g., CA1 or L5) that typically have a long or once bifurcating main apical trunk, the primary apical trunk of CA3PCs bifurcates after a relatively short distance into multiple higher-order intermediate branches.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about CA3PC morphology.

claim: The dendritic structure of CA3 pyramidal cells creates separate apical subtrees that may represent independent, parallel integrative units for dendritic processing.
source: This structure creates separate apical subtrees that may represent independent, parallel integrative units for dendritic processing, allowing interactions between the radially layered inputs: detonator-type MF synapses onto proximal trunks in str. lucidum, recurrent/associative inputs onto str. radiatum dendrites, and long-range EC inputs targeting distal apical branches in str. lacunosum-moleculare.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the morphological structure of CA3PCs.

claim: Subthreshold steady-state voltage signals attenuated more strongly from dendrite to soma than from soma to dendrite in CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: Subthreshold steady-state voltage signals attenuated more strongly from dendrite to soma than from soma to dendrite (Figure 1b and d, n = 15, p=0.004, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and d.

claim: Backpropagating action potentials were observed in almost all CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites by sufficient somatic or dendritic depolarizing stimuli.
source: bAPs could be observed in almost all dendrites both by sufficient somatic or dendritic depolarizing stimuli; they followed somatic APs with short latency, their amplitude decreased gradually with distance after the first ~150 μm (Kim et al., 2012), and they displayed a sharp initiation profile ('kink,' Gidon et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2013) and short duration, all characteristic for bAPs (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citations (Kim et al., 2012; Gidon et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2013).

claim: The amplitude of backpropagating action potentials in CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites decreased gradually with distance after the first ~150 μm.
source: bAPs could be observed in almost all dendrites both by sufficient somatic or dendritic depolarizing stimuli; they followed somatic APs with short latency, their amplitude decreased gradually with distance after the first ~150 μm (Kim et al., 2012), and they displayed a sharp initiation profile ('kink,' Gidon et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2013) and short duration, all characteristic for bAPs (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation (Kim et al., 2012).

claim: Fast dendritic Na+ spikes were generated in a subset of CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites by large current injections.
source: On the other hand, fast dendritic Na+ spikes were generated in a subset of experiments (n = 4) by large (Iinj; ≥ 600 pA) current injections into the dendrite.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dendritic recordings.

claim: Fast dendritic Na+ spikes appeared with very short latency (<7 ms) on the initial depolarizing phase of the step and attenuated strongly from dendrite to the soma.
source: These events appeared with very short latency (<7 ms) on the initial depolarizing phase of the step and attenuated strongly from dendrite to the soma (Figure 1h–j), as previously described (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h–j and citation (Kim et al., 2012).

claim: Both backpropagating action potentials and fast dendritic Na+ spikes disappeared after application of 1 μM tetrodotoxin.
source: Both of these fast spike types disappeared after the application of 1 μM tetrodotoxin (TTX) in the bath, confirming that they were mediated by VGNCs (Figure 1j, n = 12 experiments; local spikes were present in two of these experiments under control conditions; see also later the effect of TTX in single-site dendritic recordings).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: In the majority of dual recordings (17 of 21), slower regenerative voltage responses that were putative dendritic Ca2+ spikes were observed.
source: In the majority of dual recordings (17 of 21), we also observed slower regenerative voltage responses that we considered to be putative dendritic Ca2+ spikes (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Putative Ca2+ spikes in CA3 pyramidal cells were elicited with relatively longer latency or at the steady-state depolarized phase and had highly heterogeneous kinetics.
source: These spikes were elicited with relatively longer latency or at the steady-state depolarized phase, and had highly heterogeneous kinetics (see below).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from dendritic recordings.

claim: Putative Ca2+ spikes in CA3 pyramidal cells were classified into two broad groups based on their initiation characteristics: ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes.
source: We classified putative Ca2+ spikes into two broad groups based on their initiation characteristics. The first, 'classical' group consisted of regenerative ADP forms, that is, responses that followed a bAP with an additional voltage peak (Figure 2b–d). ADPs had a wide range of kinetics. In some dendrites, the ADP manifested as a sustained depolarization that triggered additional APs and gradually built up a prolonged, slowly decaying ADP driving a burst of APs ('slow ADP,' >~ 50–100 ms, Figure 2b). In other cases, the ADP occurred as a transient regenerative voltage response following 1–3 APs ('fast ADP,' Figure 2c and d), which either remained subthreshold or evoked additional AP(s) at the soma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b–d.

claim: Slow ADPs manifested as a sustained depolarization that triggered additional action potentials and gradually built up a prolonged, slowly decaying ADP driving a burst of action potentials.
source: In some dendrites, the ADP manifested as a sustained depolarization that triggered additional APs and gradually built up a prolonged, slowly decaying ADP driving a burst of APs ('slow ADP,' >~ 50–100 ms, Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Fast ADPs occurred as a transient regenerative voltage response following 1–3 action potentials.
source: In other cases, the ADP occurred as a transient regenerative voltage response following 1–3 APs ('fast ADP,' Figure 2c and d), which either remained subthreshold or evoked additional AP(s) at the soma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes were generated without an initiating backpropagating action potential.
source: In addition to 'classical' ADPs, we discovered a second, unconventional form of putative Ca2+ spikes. These events were generated without an initiating bAP and were therefore termed dendritically initiated (DI) spikes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from dendritic recordings.

claim: The rise of dendritically initiated spikes typically followed a concave, gradually developing profile that could be well distinguished from the sharp 'kink' of backpropagating action potentials.
source: The rise of these spikes typically followed a concave, gradually developing profile that could be well distinguished from the sharp 'kink' of bAPs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–e.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes could be evoked in isolation in the dendrite without evoking a backpropagating action potential.
source: Although DI spikes did not require bAPs for their initiation and could be evoked in isolation in the dendrite (Figure 2e and f), they could also evoke consecutive bAP (Figure 2g and h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and f.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes could evoke consecutive backpropagating action potentials.
source: Although DI spikes did not require bAPs for their initiation and could be evoked in isolation in the dendrite (Figure 2e and f), they could also evoke consecutive bAP (Figure 2g and h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g and h.

claim: The dendritic origin of both ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes was confirmed by their strong attenuation towards the soma.
source: The dendritic origin of both ADPs and DI spikes was confirmed by their strong attenuation towards the soma (Figure 2i and j, dendrite-soma attenuation ratio: ADPs: 5.06 ± 1.28, n = 7; DI spikes: 6.97 ± 1.09, n = 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2i and j.

claim: ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes co-occurred in some of the recordings.
source: ADPs and DI spikes co-occurred in some of the recordings (Figure 2k).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2k.

claim: All forms of putative Ca2+ spikes were accompanied by large distal dendritic Ca2+ signals that coincided with the onset of the voltage response.
source: All forms of the above-identified putative Ca2+ spikes (but not local Na+ spikes, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) were accompanied by large distal dendritic Ca2+ signals that coincided with the onset of the voltage response (Figure 2b, c, e and g), suggesting that the voltage signals propagated actively and involved regenerative Ca2+ influx.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b, c, e and g, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Local Na+ spikes were not accompanied by large distal dendritic Ca2+ signals.
source: All forms of the above-identified putative Ca2+ spikes (but not local Na+ spikes, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) were accompanied by large distal dendritic Ca2+ signals that coincided with the onset of the voltage response (Figure 2b, c, e and g), suggesting that the voltage signals propagated actively and involved regenerative Ca2+ influx.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: In single-site dendritic recordings, 1-s-long dendritic current injection steps elicited different types of putative Ca2+ spikes (ADPs and/or DI spikes) in the majority (~85%) of individual dendrites.
source: Replicating the findings of dual recordings, 1-s-long dendritic Iinj steps elicited different types of putative Ca2+ spikes, that is, ADPs and/or DI spikes in the majority (~85%) of individual dendrites, in addition to bAPs and dendritic Na+ spikes (Figure 3a–d and f, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a–d and f, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Putative Ca2+ spikes were often generated repetitively, and in some cells their kinetics were variable even across repetitions.
source: Putative Ca2+ spikes were often generated repetitively, and in some cells their kinetics were variable even across repetitions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The putative Ca2+ spikes were unaffected by blockade of AMPA and NMDA receptors.
source: The spikes were unaffected by blockade of AMPA and NMDA receptors, confirming that they were not related to excitatory synaptic activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: ADPs were expressed in 56% of investigated CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites in the 300–600 pA current injection range.
source: In a set of dendrites, we systematically determined the propensity of the two main Ca2+ spike types evoked in the 300–600 pA Iinj range, and we found that ADPs and DI spikes were expressed in 56 and 53% of the investigated dendrites, respectively (Figure 3f, n = 70 cells, dual- and single-site experiments pooled), and in 24% they both were present.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes were expressed in 53% of investigated CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites in the 300–600 pA current injection range.
source: In a set of dendrites, we systematically determined the propensity of the two main Ca2+ spike types evoked in the 300–600 pA Iinj range, and we found that ADPs and DI spikes were expressed in 56 and 53% of the investigated dendrites, respectively (Figure 3f, n = 70 cells, dual- and single-site experiments pooled), and in 24% they both were present.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: In 24% of investigated CA3 pyramidal cell dendrites, both ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes were present.
source: In a set of dendrites, we systematically determined the propensity of the two main Ca2+ spike types evoked in the 300–600 pA Iinj range, and we found that ADPs and DI spikes were expressed in 56 and 53% of the investigated dendrites, respectively (Figure 3f, n = 70 cells, dual- and single-site experiments pooled), and in 24% they both were present.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The dominant Ca2+ spike type often depended on the current injection level, with ADPs evoked at smaller and dendritically initiated spikes evoked at higher current injection.
source: The dominant Ca2+ spike type often depended on the Iinj level, with ADPs evoked at smaller and DI spikes evoked at higher Iinj (Figure 3c and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and f.

claim: In some dendrites, different Ca2+ spike types occurred intermingled within the same depolarizing trace.
source: Furthermore, in some dendrites different Ca2+ spike types occurred intermingled within the same depolarizing trace (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Both ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes were associated with large Ca2+ signals measured in dendritic segments distal to the patch pipette.
source: As in dual recordings, both ADPs and DI spikes were associated with large Ca2+ signals measured in dendritic segments > 80 μm (mean ± SEM: 215 ± 9 μm) distal to the patch pipette (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Bath application of 200 μM Ni2+ eliminated all types of putative Ca2+ spikes, whereas backpropagating action potentials and dendritic Na+ spikes were spared.
source: Bath application of 200 μM Ni2+ eliminated all types of putative Ca2+ spikes, whereas bAPs and dendritic Na+ spikes were spared (Figure 3e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels play a fundamental role in mediating ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes.
source: These results confirmed that VGCCs played a fundamental role in mediating ADPs and DI spikes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the elimination of Ca2+ spikes by Ni2+, a VGCC blocker.

claim: The amplitude of dendritically initiated spikes, measured at threshold current injection, was larger (25.4 ± 1.7 mV, n = 30) than that of fast ADPs (16.2 ± 1.8 mV, n = 18).
source: Interestingly, the amplitude of DI spikes, measured at threshold Iinj (see Materials and methods for amplitude measurement criteria), was larger (25.4 ± 1.7 mV, n = 30) than that of fast ADPs (16.2 ± 1.8 mV, n = 18; Mann–Whitney test p=0.003, Figure 3g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The difference in amplitude between dendritically initiated spikes and fast ADPs was not explained by different dendritic distance of the recordings from the soma.
source: This difference was not explained by different dendritic distance of the recordings from the soma (DI spikes: 259 ± 12 μm, ADPs: 243 ± 10 μm, Mann–Whitney test p=0.601, Figure 3h), and the amplitude of neither spike type correlated with distance (Spearman correlation: ADP: R = −0.260, p=0.296, n = 18; DI: R = −0.297, p=0.110, n = 30), suggesting a difference in the spike generation mechanism rather than simple distance-dependent variation of spike properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3h and statistical analysis.

claim: At proximal dendritic locations (<~150 μm from soma), somatic action potentials were always evoked first by dendritic depolarization.
source: When the patch pipette was positioned at relatively proximal dendritic locations (<~150 μm from soma), somatic APs were always evoked first by dendritic depolarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from dendritic recordings.

claim: At more distal dendritic locations, dendritically initiated Ca2+ spikes were often evoked before backpropagating action potentials, and this propensity depended on the strength of current injection.
source: However, at more distal dendritic locations DI Ca2+ spikes were often evoked before bAPs, and this propensity depended on the strength of Iinj (Figure 3i, ratio at 300 pA: 0.13 ± 0.04, n = 70; 400 pA: 0.26 ± 0.05, n = 75; 500 pA: 0.38 ± 0.05, n = 82; p=0.001, Kruskal–Wallis test) but was independent from the distance from soma (Figure 3j, Spearman correlation R = −0.031, p=0.778, n = 82).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3i and j.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes can be evoked efficiently by local depolarization of medial-distal apical trunks of CA3 pyramidal cells without any preceding somatic activity.
source: Thus, DI spikes can be evoked efficiently by local depolarization of medial-distal apical trunks of CA3PCs without any preceding somatic activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing DI spikes evoked before bAPs.

claim: Synaptic stimulation using two-photon glutamate uncaging was able to elicit characteristic and well-distinguishable ADPs and dendritically initiated spikes.
source: Synaptic stimulation was able to elicit characteristic and well-distinguishable ADPs and DI spikes (Figure 3n) either separately (ADP only: 3/10 dendrites, Figure 3l; DI spike only: 4/10 dendrites, Figure 3m) or in combination (1/10 dendrites).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3l, m, and n.

claim: The Ca2+ spike profile of the dendrite evoked by glutamate uncaging was similar to that seen with current injection via the pipette.
source: The Ca2+ spike profile of the dendrite evoked by uncaging was similar to that seen with Iinj via the pipette (Figure 3l and m), and DI spikes had amplitudes comparable to that typically evoked by Iinj (Figure 3o).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3l, m, and o.

claim: The Ca2+ spike form is an inherent property of the dendrite, and separate Ca2+ spike modes can be elicited by a wide range of stimuli that reach sufficiently strong local depolarization.

claim: In most CA1 pyramidal cells, dendritic depolarization by 300–600 pA current injection evoked voltage-gated Ca2+ channel-mediated ADPs.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–c, d, and g.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes were not observed in CA1 pyramidal cell trunks.
source: Furthermore, DI spikes were not observed in CA1PC trunks (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e), and accordingly, bAPs were always evoked before Ca2+ spikes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3e and f.

claim: Backpropagating action potentials were always evoked before Ca2+ spikes in CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Furthermore, DI spikes were not observed in CA1PC trunks (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e), and accordingly, bAPs were always evoked before Ca2+ spikes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3f.

claim: Active properties of CA3 pyramidal cell trunk dendrites fundamentally differ from those of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Thus, active properties of CA3PC trunk dendrites fundamentally differ from those of CA1PCs, indicating that the repertoire and roles of dendritic computation can vary in different types of rat PCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of dendritic properties between CA3PCs and CA1PCs.

claim: The repertoire and roles of dendritic computation can vary in different types of rat pyramidal cells.
source: Thus, active properties of CA3PC trunk dendrites fundamentally differ from those of CA1PCs, indicating that the repertoire and roles of dendritic computation can vary in different types of rat PCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in dendritic properties between CA3PCs and CA1PCs.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes in CA3 pyramidal cells share several properties with a novel type of Ca2+ spikes in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells, including backpropagating action potential-independent initiation, fast rise, and large amplitude.
source: Curiously, however, some features of CA3PC dendritic Ca2+ spikes resembled those recently described in L2/3PCs in cortical slices removed from human patients (hL2/3PCs; Gidon et al., 2020). Specifically, the DI spikes we observed in CA3PCs shared several properties with a novel type of Ca2+ spikes in hL2/3 PCs: they were characterized by bAP-independent initiation, fast rise and large amplitude (Figure 4a and b), which inversely scaled with increasing Iinj (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a–e and citation (Gidon et al., 2020).

claim: The amplitude of dendritically initiated spikes inversely scaled with increasing current injection.
source: Specifically, the DI spikes we observed in CA3PCs shared several properties with a novel type of Ca2+ spikes in hL2/3 PCs: they were characterized by bAP-independent initiation, fast rise and large amplitude (Figure 4a and b), which inversely scaled with increasing Iinj (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c–e.

claim: In some dendrites, the depolarization level-dependent reduction in amplitude of dendritically initiated spikes created a window of dendritic stimulus strength where action potentials could be specifically triggered by these dendritic events.
source: In some dendrites (6 out of 12 tested), the depolarization level-dependent reduction in amplitude created a window of dendritic stimulus strength where APs could be specifically triggered by these dendritic events (Figure 4f), similarly to that described in hL2/3PCs (Gidon et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f and citation (Gidon et al., 2020).

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes are expressed in specific neuron types of various species including humans and rats.
source: We conclude that DI spikes are expressed in specific neuron types of various species including humans and rats.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarities between DI spikes in rat CA3PCs and human L2/3PCs.

claim: Bath application of tetrodotoxin completely eliminated backpropagating action potentials and Na+ spikes, whereas putative Ca2+ spikes persisted.
source: As expected, TTX completely eliminated bAPs and Na+ spikes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h and i, see also Figure 1), whereas putative Ca2+ spikes, associated with large dendritic Ca2+ signals, persisted.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h and i, and Figure 1.

claim: In dendrites that under control conditions expressed only ADPs but no dendritically initiated spikes, tetrodotoxin-resistant Ca2+ spikes were typically slow.
source: The kinetics of the regenerative spikes remaining in TTX varied in a wide range, but mirrored the behavior in control conditions. That is, in dendrites that under control conditions expressed only ADPs (fast or slow) but no DI spikes, TTX-resistant Ca2+ spikes were typically slow (Figure 5a and c, width: 166.6 ± 26.8 ms, n = 12), whereas those dendrites that fired DI spikes (with or without ADPs) under control conditions displayed dominantly fast, transient, TTX-resistant Ca2+ spikes (Figure 5b and c, width: 9.3 ± 0.7 ms, n = 13, Mann–Whitney test p<0.001), although a smaller slow component was often also present.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a and c.

claim: Dendrites that fired dendritically initiated spikes under control conditions displayed dominantly fast, transient, tetrodotoxin-resistant Ca2+ spikes.
source: The kinetics of the regenerative spikes remaining in TTX varied in a wide range, but mirrored the behavior in control conditions. That is, in dendrites that under control conditions expressed only ADPs (fast or slow) but no DI spikes, TTX-resistant Ca2+ spikes were typically slow (Figure 5a and c, width: 166.6 ± 26.8 ms, n = 12), whereas those dendrites that fired DI spikes (with or without ADPs) under control conditions displayed dominantly fast, transient, TTX-resistant Ca2+ spikes (Figure 5b and c, width: 9.3 ± 0.7 ms, n = 13, Mann–Whitney test p<0.001), although a smaller slow component was often also present.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: The duration of tetrodotoxin-resistant Ca2+ spikes in CA3 pyramidal cells clearly separated from those of CA1 pyramidal cell dendrites under similar conditions.
source: The duration of TTX-resistant Ca2+ spikes in CA3PCs clearly separated from those of CA1PC dendrites under similar conditions (width: 39.4 ± 5.1 ms, n = 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 3h and i), further confirming cell-type-specific differences in Ca2+ spike properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3h and i.

claim: In ~25% of dendrites, no clear regenerative voltage responses could be evoked after tetrodotoxin application.
source: Finally, in ~25% of dendrites, no clear regenerative voltage responses could be evoked after TTX application (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels play a fundamental role in generating a wide kinetic range of Ca2+ spikes in CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: These results, together with the elimination of all types of Ca2+ spikes by 200 μM Ni2+ (Figure 3e), confirm a fundamental role of VGCCs in generating a wide kinetic range of Ca2+ spikes in CA3PCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effects of TTX and Ni2+ on Ca2+ spikes.

claim: The amplitude of tetrodotoxin-resistant fast spikes was consistently smaller than that of the dendritically initiated spikes in artificial cerebrospinal fluid.
source: To our surprise, we noticed that the amplitude (and dV/dt) of TTX-resistant fast spikes was consistently smaller than that of the DI spikes in ACSF (in ACSF: 26.9 ± 2.2 mV, in TTX: 8.2 ± 1.0 mV, n = 17, Wilcoxon test, p<0.001), whereas the amplitudes of ADPs and TTX-resistant slow spikes were not systematically different (17.2 ± 2.6 mV before and 15.9 ± 2.4 mV after TTX application, n = 7, p=0.735, Wilcoxon test, Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The amplitudes of ADPs and tetrodotoxin-resistant slow spikes were not systematically different.
source: To our surprise, we noticed that the amplitude (and dV/dt) of TTX-resistant fast spikes was consistently smaller than that of the DI spikes in ACSF (in ACSF: 26.9 ± 2.2 mV, in TTX: 8.2 ± 1.0 mV, n = 17, Wilcoxon test, p<0.001), whereas the amplitudes of ADPs and TTX-resistant slow spikes were not systematically different (17.2 ± 2.6 mV before and 15.9 ± 2.4 mV after TTX application, n = 7, p=0.735, Wilcoxon test, Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The reduction of dendritically initiated spike amplitude by tetrodotoxin was largely caused by a drop in peak voltage rather than a modest increase in spike threshold.
source: Our analysis showed that the reduction of spike amplitude was largely caused by a drop in peak voltage (from –0.8 ± 2.2 mV to –15.6 ± 1.3 mV, n = 17, p<0.001, Wilcoxon test, Figure 5—figure supplement 1d) rather than the modest increase in spike threshold (from –27.2 ± 1.0 mV to –23.7 ± 1.0 mV, n = 17, p<0.01, Wilcoxon test, Figure 5—figure supplement 1e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d, e, and f.

claim: Tetrodotoxin did not affect the initial slow, concave rise of the dendritically initiated spike, but exclusively reduced the subsequent, fast-rising peak component.
source: Furthermore, overlaying individual traces (Figure 5e) or aligning averaged voltage responses in control and TTX to a specific dV/dt value (1 V/s; Figure 5f) revealed that TTX did not affect the initial slow, concave rise of the spike, but exclusively reduced the subsequent, fast-rising peak component.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e and f.

claim: Replacement of a majority of extracellular Na+ ions in the artificial cerebrospinal fluid with NMDG+ produced a similar effect to that of tetrodotoxin on dendritically initiated spikes.
source: As an independent confirmation of the involvement of VGNCs in the generation of DI spikes, replacement of a majority of extracellular Na+ ions in the ACSF with the large cation NMDG+ (which permeates less through VGNCs) produced a similar effect to that of TTX (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c and g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c and g.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes can be mediated by a hybrid mechanism, whereby initiation of a fast Ca2+ spike can recruit regenerative activation of voltage-gated Na+ channels that further amplify and sharpen the voltage response.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that DI spikes can be mediated by a hybrid mechanism, whereby initiation of a fast Ca2+ spike can recruit regenerative activation of VGNCs that further amplify and sharpen the voltage response, with the two components blending smoothly into a rapid and transient combined dendritic spike.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effects of TTX and NMDG+ on DI spikes.

claim: Slow Ca2+ spikes were accompanied by large Ca2+ signals both in the patched dendritic family and in another dendrite branching off more proximally from a different low-order trunk segment.
source: We found a strong difference between fast and slow spikes in their propagation properties (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, p<0.001 for kinetic group, p=0.005 for location, p<0.001 for interaction). Slow Ca2+ spikes (width >60 ms) were accompanied by large (likely dye-saturating) Ca2+ signals both in d1 and d2 (Figure 6b and c, n = 5 cells, p=0.781, Tukey's post hoc test), and even in basal dendrites (measured in n = 3 cells, Figure 6d), indicating efficient propagation across major bifurcation points or even the entire dendritic tree.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b, c, and d.

claim: Slow Ca2+ spikes indicate efficient propagation across major bifurcation points or even the entire dendritic tree.
source: Slow Ca2+ spikes (width >60 ms) were accompanied by large (likely dye-saturating) Ca2+ signals both in d1 and d2 (Figure 6b and c, n = 5 cells, p=0.781, Tukey's post hoc test), and even in basal dendrites (measured in n = 3 cells, Figure 6d), indicating efficient propagation across major bifurcation points or even the entire dendritic tree.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the widespread Ca2+ signals associated with slow Ca2+ spikes.

claim: Fast Ca2+ spikes were restricted to the dendritic family connected to the patched trunk.
source: In contrast, fast Ca2+ spikes (width <20 ms) were restricted to the dendritic family connected to the patched trunk (Figure 6b and c; n = 9 cells, p<0.001, Tukey's post hoc test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b and c.

claim: Fast Ca2+ spikes evoked relatively uniform, large Ca2+ signals towards distal dendritic locations, but a strong drop of Ca2+ signals within ~160 μm from the pipette in the proximal direction.
source: Finally, to assess the local propagation capacity of fast Ca2+ spikes in more detail, we mapped fast Ca2+ spike-associated Ca2+ signals in higher spatial resolution proximally and distally from the patch pipette (using the low-affinity Ca2+ dye OGB-6F to reduce complications from dye saturation). These experiments revealed relatively uniform, large Ca2+ signals towards distal dendritic locations, but a strong drop of Ca2+ signals within ~160 μm from the pipette in the proximal direction, so that fast spikes evoked in a higher-order trunk did not propagate closer than ~100 μm to the soma (Figure 6d–f, n = 4 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d–f.

claim: Fast spikes evoked in a higher-order trunk did not propagate closer than ~100 μm to the soma.
source: These experiments revealed relatively uniform, large Ca2+ signals towards distal dendritic locations, but a strong drop of Ca2+ signals within ~160 μm from the pipette in the proximal direction, so that fast spikes evoked in a higher-order trunk did not propagate closer than ~100 μm to the soma (Figure 6d–f, n = 4 experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d–f.

claim: Slow Ca2+ spikes are global events that engage virtually the entire dendritic tree.
source: These results indicate different generation and propagation properties of different Ca2+ spike types (Figure 6g). Slow Ca2+ spikes are apparently global events that engage virtually the entire dendritic tree.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the widespread Ca2+ signals associated with slow Ca2+ spikes.

claim: Fast Ca2+ spikes are generated within the dendritic family of the stimulated trunk, and although they propagate well distally, they cannot efficiently invade the proximal main or sibling trunk segments.
source: In contrast, fast Ca2+ spikes are generated within the dendritic family of the stimulated trunk, and although they propagate well distally, they cannot efficiently invade the proximal main or sibling trunk segments, creating a mesoscale compartmentalization level represented by separate apical dendritic subtrees.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial restriction of Ca2+ signals associated with fast Ca2+ spikes.

claim: Fast Ca2+ spikes create a mesoscale compartmentalization level represented by separate apical dendritic subtrees.
source: In contrast, fast Ca2+ spikes are generated within the dendritic family of the stimulated trunk, and although they propagate well distally, they cannot efficiently invade the proximal main or sibling trunk segments, creating a mesoscale compartmentalization level represented by separate apical dendritic subtrees.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial restriction of Ca2+ signals associated with fast Ca2+ spikes.

claim: The dendritic structure of CA3 pyramidal cells is highly diverse.
source: The dendritic structure of CA3PCs is highly diverse, and their electrophysiological properties were proposed to be related to their topographic position within the CA3 area and dendritic morphology (Bilkey and Schwartzkroin, 1990; Ding et al., 2020; Hunt et al., 2018; Raus Balind et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Bilkey and Schwartzkroin, 1990; Ding et al., 2020; Hunt et al., 2018; Raus Balind et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017).

claim: The electrophysiological properties of CA3 pyramidal cells were proposed to be related to their topographic position within the CA3 area and dendritic morphology.
source: The dendritic structure of CA3PCs is highly diverse, and their electrophysiological properties were proposed to be related to their topographic position within the CA3 area and dendritic morphology (Bilkey and Schwartzkroin, 1990; Ding et al., 2020; Hunt et al., 2018; Raus Balind et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Bilkey and Schwartzkroin, 1990; Ding et al., 2020; Hunt et al., 2018; Raus Balind et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017).

claim: A recent study suggested the existence of a sparse class of CA3 pyramidal cells with bursting phenotype that lack thorny excrescences.
source: A recent study even suggested the existence of a sparse class of CA3PCs with bursting phenotype that lack thorny excrescences (TEs) and input from mossy fibers ('athorny' cells, Hunt et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Hunt et al., 2018).

claim: In almost all fluorescently labeled CA3 pyramidal cells, the presence of thorny excrescences was unambiguously confirmed.
source: In almost all of our fluorescently labeled cells, we unambiguously confirmed the presence of TEs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from morphological analysis.

claim: The estimated coverage of the proximal trunk(s) by thorny excrescences varied widely and was inversely correlated with the length of first-order apical trunk(s).
source: The estimated coverage of the proximal trunk(s) by TEs varied widely (Figure 7a and b) and was inversely correlated with the length of first-order apical trunk(s) (Figure 7c, Spearman correlation R = −0.495, p<0.001, n = 89), confirming previous studies (Fitch et al., 1989) and suggesting a gradient of morpho-functional properties of regular CA3PCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a, b, and c, and citation (Fitch et al., 1989).

claim: The dendritic Ca2+ spike profile was correlated with basic anatomical features of CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: We found that the dendritic Ca2+ spike profile was correlated with these basic anatomical features of CA3PCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlations between spike types and morphological features.

claim: CA3 pyramidal cells expressing dendritically initiated spikes had on average twice as high thorny excrescence coverage as ADP-only cells.
source: First, CA3PCs expressing DI spikes in the recorded dendrite (with or without ADPs) had on average twice as high TE coverage (Figure 7d, ADP-only: 40 ± 5 μm, n = 19; DI: 84 ± 8 μm, n = 35, Mann–Whitney test: p<0.001) than ADP-only cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Cells with dendritically initiated spikes had shorter primary trunks than ADP-only cells.
source: Second, cells with DI spikes had shorter primary trunks (Figure 7e, ADP-only: 128 ± 11 μm, n = 20; DI: 57 ± 5 μm, n = 41, Mann–Whitney test: p=0.002) and more often had multiple first-order trunks (Figure 7f, ADP-only: 1 ± 0, n = 20; DI: 1.49 ± 0.11, n = 41, Mann–Whitney test: p<0.001) than ADP-only cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Cells with dendritically initiated spikes more often had multiple first-order trunks than ADP-only cells.
source: Second, cells with DI spikes had shorter primary trunks (Figure 7e, ADP-only: 128 ± 11 μm, n = 20; DI: 57 ± 5 μm, n = 41, Mann–Whitney test: p=0.002) and more often had multiple first-order trunks (Figure 7f, ADP-only: 1 ± 0, n = 20; DI: 1.49 ± 0.11, n = 41, Mann–Whitney test: p<0.001) than ADP-only cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The dendritic path between the pipette and soma contained more branch points in the case of dendrites with dendritically initiated spikes compared to ADP-only dendrites.
source: Interestingly, although the distance of the dendritic patch pipette from the soma was similar in the two electrophysiological groups (ADP-only: 276 ± 15 μm, n = 20; DI: 260 ± 10 μm, n = 41, Mann–Whitney test: p=0.282, see also Figure 3h), the dendritic path between the pipette and soma contained more branch points in the case of dendrites with DI spikes (Figure 7g, ADP-only: 4.15 ± 0.36, n = 20; DI: 5.97 ± 0.35, n = 39, Mann–Whitney test: p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: The morphological diversity of CA3 pyramidal cells corresponds to distinct dendritic excitability phenotypes.
source: In summary, the morphological diversity of CA3PCs corresponds to distinct dendritic excitability phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlations between morphological features and Ca2+ spike types.

claim: ADP-type Ca2+ spikes often triggered additional somatic spike(s) to produce short or long series of action potentials or bursts after the first initiating action potential.
source: ADP-type Ca2+ spikes indeed served such a role: they often triggered additional somatic spike(s) to produce short (2–3 APs) or long (>3 APs) series of APs or bursts after the first initiating AP (Figure 8a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a and b.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes never evoked more than a single somatic action potential.
source: In contrast, DI spikes never evoked more than a single somatic AP (Figure 8a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a–c.

claim: Compared to simple backpropagating action potentials, the backpropagating action potential evoked by dendritically initiated spikes was followed by a faster repolarization rate in the dendrites.
source: Furthermore, compared to simple bAPs (s-APs), the bAP evoked by DI spikes (Ca-APs) was followed by a faster repolarization rate (ratio of dV/dtmin (Ca-APs/s-APs): 1.29 ± 0.04, p=0.001, Wilcoxon test compared to 1) and enhanced fast afterhyperpolarization (difference of AHP Vmin (Ca-AP ˗ s-AP): –2.68 ± 0.34 mV, p=0.001, Wilcoxon test compared to 0) in the dendrites (n = 13, pooled dual [n = 5] and dendrite-only [n = 8] recordings, Figure 8c–e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) as well as larger AHP at the soma (s-AP: –3.21 ± 0.89 mV, Ca-AP: –4.70 ± 1.12 mV, measured in n = 5 dual recordings, p=0.043, Wilcoxon test, Figure 8c, d and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c–e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The backpropagating action potential evoked by dendritically initiated spikes was followed by enhanced fast afterhyperpolarization in the dendrites.
source: Furthermore, compared to simple bAPs (s-APs), the bAP evoked by DI spikes (Ca-APs) was followed by a faster repolarization rate (ratio of dV/dtmin (Ca-APs/s-APs): 1.29 ± 0.04, p=0.001, Wilcoxon test compared to 1) and enhanced fast afterhyperpolarization (difference of AHP Vmin (Ca-AP ˗ s-AP): –2.68 ± 0.34 mV, p=0.001, Wilcoxon test compared to 0) in the dendrites (n = 13, pooled dual [n = 5] and dendrite-only [n = 8] recordings, Figure 8c–e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) as well as larger AHP at the soma (s-AP: –3.21 ± 0.89 mV, Ca-AP: –4.70 ± 1.12 mV, measured in n = 5 dual recordings, p=0.043, Wilcoxon test, Figure 8c, d and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c–e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The backpropagating action potential evoked by dendritically initiated spikes was followed by larger afterhyperpolarization at the soma.
source: Furthermore, compared to simple bAPs (s-APs), the bAP evoked by DI spikes (Ca-APs) was followed by a faster repolarization rate (ratio of dV/dtmin (Ca-APs/s-APs): 1.29 ± 0.04, p=0.001, Wilcoxon test compared to 1) and enhanced fast afterhyperpolarization (difference of AHP Vmin (Ca-AP ˗ s-AP): –2.68 ± 0.34 mV, p=0.001, Wilcoxon test compared to 0) in the dendrites (n = 13, pooled dual [n = 5] and dendrite-only [n = 8] recordings, Figure 8c–e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) as well as larger AHP at the soma (s-AP: –3.21 ± 0.89 mV, Ca-AP: –4.70 ± 1.12 mV, measured in n = 5 dual recordings, p=0.043, Wilcoxon test, Figure 8c, d and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c, d and f.

claim: The impact of dendritically initiated spikes on somatic output is the opposite of that classically proposed for dendritic Ca2+ spikes: they not only trigger strictly single action potentials, but they even suppress the probability of consecutive action potential generation and thereby actively reduce burst output.
source: Thus, the impact of DI spikes on somatic output is the opposite of that classically proposed for dendritic Ca2+ spikes: they not only trigger strictly single APs, but they even suppress the probability of consecutive AP generation and thereby actively reduce burst output.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing single AP output and enhanced AHP following DI spikes.

claim: Slow Ca2+ spikes are primarily responsible for generating afterdepolarization following initial action potential(s) and evoke bursts of additional action potentials at the soma.
source: One prominent component is provided by slow Ca2+ spikes, which are primarily responsible for generating ADP following initial AP(s) and evoke bursts of additional APs at the soma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing ADPs and burst firing.

claim: The slow Ca2+ spikes underlying ADPs in CA3 pyramidal cells are typically longer lasting (on average approximately threefold) than similar type Ca2+ spikes in CA1 pyramidal cell trunks.
source: We found that the slow Ca2+ spikes underlying ADPs in CA3PCs are typically longer lasting (on average approximately threefold) than similar type Ca2+ spikes in CA1PC trunks.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing CA3PCs and CA1PCs.

claim: Slow Ca2+ spikes are most prevalent in CA3 pyramidal cells with relatively long single primary trunks.
source: We also showed that slow Ca2+ spikes appear globally throughout the apical (or even the whole) dendritic arbor, and they are most prevalent in CA3PCs with relatively long single primary trunks.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between slow Ca2+ spikes and morphology.

claim: The properties of slow Ca2+ spikes align with the high burst propensity observed in deep distal CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: These properties altogether well align with the high burst propensity observed in deep distal CA3PCs, which show this morphological feature (Hunt et al., 2018; Raus Balind et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between slow Ca2+ spikes, morphology, and burst propensity, supported by citations (Hunt et al., 2018; Raus Balind et al., 2019).

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes are generated by fast Ca2+ spikes, which, if large enough, can recruit subsequent contribution by regenerative voltage-gated Na+ channel activation.
source: In addition to slow Ca2+ spikes, depolarization also evoked a novel fast form of DI spikes in a large fraction of CA3PC trunk dendrites. DI spikes are generated by fast Ca2+ spikes, which, if large enough, can recruit subsequent contribution by regenerative VGNC activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the hybrid mechanism of DI spikes.

claim: When combined into a hybrid dendritic spike, fast Ca2+ spikes can produce large enough depolarization in a window above threshold stimulation to efficiently evoke a tightly coupled action potential at the soma.
source: Especially when combined into such hybrid d-spike, fast Ca2+ spikes can produce large enough depolarization in a window above threshold stimulation to efficiently evoke a tightly coupled AP at the soma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing AP generation by DI spikes.

claim: Action potentials evoked by dendritically initiated spikes are immediately followed by enhanced repolarization and afterhyperpolarization both at dendrite and soma, cutting off depolarization and actively blocking burst firing.
source: Curiously, these APs are immediately followed by enhanced repolarization and AHP both at dendrite and soma, cutting off depolarization and actively blocking burst firing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing enhanced repolarization and AHP following DI spikes.

claim: The regular spiking firing profile of certain CA3 pyramidal cells may be not simply due to a lack of dendritic spikes promoting bursts, but instead due to a specific form of local dendritic spikes that actively produces non-bursting, regular spiking firing phenotype.
source: This means that the regular spiking firing profile of certain CA3PCs may be not simply due to a lack of d-spikes (or other mechanisms) promoting bursts, but instead due to a specific form of local dendritic spikes that actively produces non-bursting, regular spiking firing phenotype.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the anti-bursting effect of DI spikes.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes might serve to amplify certain local apical synaptic input forms without strong perisomatic dendritic activity to promote an output, yet they do so in a way that prevents switching to burst firing.
source: From another point of view, DI spikes might serve to amplify certain local apical synaptic input forms without strong perisomatic dendritic activity (i.e., no bAPs) to promote an output, yet they do so in a way that prevents switching to burst firing, which can be preserved for signaling different input patterns, for example, associative input conjunction (Raus Balind et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role for DI spikes, supported by citation (Raus Balind et al., 2019).

claim: Dendritic families composed of higher-order trunks with connected daughter branches can correspond to independent spatial units of synaptic integration and/or plasticity.
source: Thus, dendritic families composed of higher-order trunks with connected daughter branches can correspond to independent spatial units of synaptic integration and/or plasticity (~3–5 units per cell).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the compartmentalization of fast Ca2+ spikes.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes could be particularly suited to promote compartmentalized induction of synaptic or intrinsic plasticity.
source: One might speculate that DI spikes could be particularly suited to promote compartmentalized induction of synaptic or intrinsic (Losonczy et al., 2008) plasticity because the evoked single APs, backpropagating from the soma to other parts of the dendritic arbor, would likely be inefficient to induce substantial plasticity outside the spike-generating dendritic family.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role for DI spikes, supported by citation (Losonczy et al., 2008).

claim: Compartmentalized plasticity promoted by dendritically initiated spikes could lead to biased wiring of correlated synaptic inputs targeting specific apical subtrees.
source: Such compartmentalized plasticity could lead to biased wiring of correlated synaptic inputs targeting specific apical subtrees.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a consequence of compartmentalized plasticity.

claim: Due to their strong attenuation, dendritically initiated spikes are challenging to detect and likely remain overlooked with somatic voltage recording techniques.
source: Notably, due to their strong attenuation, DI spikes are challenging to detect and likely remain overlooked with somatic voltage recording techniques; multisite measurements in dendrites and soma, for example, with fast voltage imaging techniques will be required to uncover this form of input-output transformation in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the strong attenuation of DI spikes from dendrite to soma.

claim: It is likely that large transient ADPs observed in some dendrites were mediated by a similar fast Ca2+ spike mechanism to that producing dendritically initiated spikes.
source: While we classified the dendrites based on whether they expressed DI spikes, it is likely that large transient ADPs that we also observed in some of the dendrites were mediated by a similar fast Ca2+ spike mechanism to that producing DI spikes.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation of fast ADPs and their properties.

claim: At weaker depolarization, the arrival of a backpropagating action potential can provide the necessary stimulus to trigger the Ca2+ spike that therefore appears as an afterdepolarization.
source: We speculate that at weaker depolarization the arrival of a bAP can provide the necessary stimulus to trigger the Ca2+ spike that therefore appears as an ADP; the inactivation of VGNCs during the initializing bAP may prevent their further contribution to the spike.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for ADP generation.

claim: Stronger depolarization can itself initiate fast Ca2+ spikes, which in turn can trigger an additional Na+ spike component to develop the full fast hybrid dendritically initiated spike.
source: In contrast, stronger depolarization can itself initiate the fast Ca2+ spikes, which in turn can trigger an additional Na+ spike component to develop the full fast hybrid DI spike.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for DI spike generation.

claim: A substantial fraction of CA3 pyramidal cells coexpressed different types of Ca2+ spikes.
source: Notably, a substantial fraction of CA3PCs coexpressed different types of Ca2+ spikes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing co-occurrence of different Ca2+ spike types.

claim: The various forms of fast and slow dendritic Ca2+ spikes in the complex branching apical tree provide particularly large room for specific input-output transformations in CA3 pyramidal cells depending on the strength and actual spatiotemporal pattern of activity of the three different sources of afferent synaptic inputs.
source: Altogether, the various forms of fast and slow dendritic Ca2+ spikes in the complex branching apical tree provide particularly large room for specific input-output transformations in CA3PCs depending on the strength and actual spatiotemporal pattern of activity of the three different sources of afferent synaptic inputs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the diversity of Ca2+ spikes and the complex dendritic structure of CA3PCs.

claim: The diversity of Ca2+ spike characteristics may be explained by differences in the molecular composition or functional properties of various voltage-gated Ca2+ channel subtypes producing kinetically different Ca2+ currents.
source: In particular, future work is needed to resolve whether the diversity may be explained by differences in the molecular composition or functional properties of various VGCC subtypes producing kinetically different Ca2+ currents (Avery and Johnston, 1996) or other, particularly K+ channel types (e.g., specific voltage-dependent or Ca2+-activated K+ channels), as well as the role of passive properties.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential mechanisms for Ca2+ spike diversity, supported by citation (Avery and Johnston, 1996).

claim: The observed correlation of functional and morphological properties of CA3 pyramidal cells suggests an at least partially rigid organization of dendritic spike mechanisms in different dendritic compartments.
source: While ion channels may be regulated in an activity- or state-dependent fashion, the observed correlation of functional and morphological properties of CA3PCs suggests an at least partially rigid organization of d-spike mechanisms in different dendritic compartments (although proximal apical CA3 dendritic morphology is plastic; Juraska et al., 1989; McEwen and Magarinos, 1997).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between morphology and Ca2+ spike types, supported by citations (Juraska et al., 1989; McEwen and Magarinos, 1997).

claim: A reasonably long primary trunk appears to allow the generation of slow Ca2+ spikes with a low threshold that can be reached both by synaptic/dendritic and somatic depolarization.
source: A reasonably long primary trunk appears to allow the generation of slow Ca2+ spikes with a low threshold that can be reached both by synaptic/dendritic and somatic depolarization (Raus Balind et al., 2019), whereas higher-order trunks may be diverse individual Ca2+ spike generators.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between morphology and Ca2+ spike types, supported by citation (Raus Balind et al., 2019).

claim: Higher-order trunks may be diverse individual Ca2+ spike generators.
source: A reasonably long primary trunk appears to allow the generation of slow Ca2+ spikes with a low threshold that can be reached both by synaptic/dendritic and somatic depolarization (Raus Balind et al., 2019), whereas higher-order trunks may be diverse individual Ca2+ spike generators.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed diversity of Ca2+ spikes in higher-order trunks.

claim: The functional properties of dendritically initiated spikes discovered in rat CA3 pyramidal cells resemble those recently described for dendritic Ca2+ spikes in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells of the human neocortex.
source: The functional properties of DI spikes we discovered in rat CA3PCs resemble those recently described for dendritic Ca2+ spikes (called dCaAPs) in L2/3PCs of the human neocortex derived from patients operated for epilepsy or tumor (Gidon et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with citation (Gidon et al., 2020).

claim: The kinetics and the inverse relationship of amplitude with depolarization of dendritically initiated spikes in rat CA3 pyramidal cells was similar to that in human layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Except for somewhat different amplitudes, the kinetics and the inverse relationship of amplitude with depolarization of these spikes in rat CA3PCs was similar to that in hL2/3PCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with human L2/3PCs.

claim: The results contradict the idea that dendritically initiated Ca2+ spikes would have developed to support human specific cortical computations.
source: Altogether, our results contradict the idea that DI Ca2+ spikes would have developed to support human specific cortical computations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of DI spikes in both rat and human neurons.

claim: Dendritically initiated spikes may contribute to basic circuit computation motifs shared by hippocampal CA3 and superficial cortical pyramidal cells.
source: Instead, it is intriguing to speculate that DI spikes may contribute to basic circuit computation motifs shared by hippocampal CA3 and superficial cortical PCs, for example, related to their intermediate position in a sequential chain of input processing (Shepherd, 2011).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role for DI spikes, supported by citation (Shepherd, 2011).

claim: The presence of dendritically initiated Ca2+ spikes in neurons of healthy rats is a strong indication for their physiological role.
source: Finally, the presence of DI Ca2+ spikes in neurons of healthy rats is a strong indication for their physiological role and argues against a possibility that the expression of these spikes in human neurons could have been related to disease or pharmacological treatment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of DI spikes in healthy rat neurons.

claim: Different types of pyramidal cells may utilize different structure-function models for dendritic computations.
source: Altogether, our results point out that different types of PCs may utilize different structure-function models for dendritic computations (i.e., different architecture of hierarchical and parallel nodes of nonlinear synaptic integration) that allow complex forms of input-output transformations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in dendritic properties between different PC types.

claim: The cell-type-specific forms of dendritic spikes raise the idea that active dendrites may support circuit-specific computations.
source: The cell-type-specific forms of dendritic spikes raise the idea that active dendrites may support circuit-specific computations, whereas the heterogeneity within a principal cell class suggests that PC subpopulations may be dedicated to perform different information processing functions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional implication of cell-type-specific dendritic spikes.

claim: The heterogeneity within a principal cell class suggests that pyramidal cell subpopulations may be dedicated to perform different information processing functions.
source: The cell-type-specific forms of dendritic spikes raise the idea that active dendrites may support circuit-specific computations, whereas the heterogeneity within a principal cell class suggests that PC subpopulations may be dedicated to perform different information processing functions.
